items.excerpt: Harriman House claims a trade publishing first with The Everything Code by macro analyst Raoul Pal, produced with a proprietary AI tool trained exclusively on the author's own existing work. It is a concrete template for 'AI-facilitated' authorship — a model trained on one author's corpus, disclosed on the jacket — rather than an anonymous LLM draft.

A US class action filed by textbook authors alleges OpenAI ingested hundreds of academic volumes. The suit argues that if LLMs keep ingesting new editions as they appear, instructors may drop textbook adoptions entirely in favour of AI 'substitutes' — putting the economics of educational authorship, not just the training question, on trial.

Originality.ai scanned 2,034 paperback religion books on Amazon and found 63% were likely AI-written — 78% in witchcraft, 76% Hinduism, 74% Taoism, versus 22% in Satanism. Likely-AI titles averaged $16.84 and 170 pages against $18.96 and 208 pages for human-written ones, a measurable shape for the AI slop flooding a single retail category.

A pointed essay against the 'AI reading buddy' — the chat-with-your-book, summarise-this-chapter layer now being bolted onto ereaders and reading apps. The argument: bulletpointising books optimises away the difficulty that reading is actually for, and product teams shipping reading assistants are designing the wrong metric.

As AI licensing deals, microdeals and new-format expansions proliferate, rights systems built for a handful of annual contracts are breaking. The piece argues transparent, creator-facing rights reporting is now the trust infrastructure publishers have to build before they can sell training or AI-format rights at all.

After a run of authors were publicly suspected of using generative AI, the trade is debating whether authors of colour are disproportionately targeted by AI accusations. Vibes-based 'AI detection' is becoming an informal gatekeeping mechanism with no evidentiary standard — a direct problem for how manuscripts get screened and acquired.

A roundup of the provenance stack forming around books: Claude adding watermarks to generated text, Substack adopting Pangram AI detection, and the resulting disclosure pressure on writers. Useful as the 'who is checking what' map for anyone publishing AI-assisted prose.

Dan Holloway reports on the launch of the Indie Manga Alliance, Libro.fm's move into e-books, and new research showing readers largely cannot tell AI-written stories from human ones. The manga alliance is an organised indie-creator response to AI-assisted comics production and translation.

Part 1 of a two-part framework arguing that AI is now permanent in scholarly publishing, so the question is how it should be understood and governed rather than whether to allow it. Maps where AI mediation enters the path to editorial judgment — a governance model transferable to trade editorial workflows.

UC Berkeley mathematician Zvezdelina Stankova admits she used AI to 'help edit' a widely circulated op-ed about students' math skills. A live test case for where the line sits between AI line-editing and AI authorship — the same disclosure question editors and publishers are now writing into contracts.

Platforms are finally acting on the fact that audiences don't want AI slop: a growing number of sites and apps now flag, label or ban AI-generated content outright. The labelling wave landing on storefronts and reading platforms reshapes how AI-assisted books and covers can be listed and sold.

ALLi's read on Anthropic watermarking Claude's text output, framed for indie authors: what invisible provenance marks mean for AI-assisted manuscripts, retailer disclosure rules, and whether an editing pass leaves a trace in a finished book.

Digital Publishing Report opens its industry survey asking which publishing technologies executives should watch, pilot or scale — an explicit attempt to separate AI experiments that are ready to be operationalised from those that are still demos. Survey closes August 30.

A refreshed 2026 comparison of proofreading tools for authors — Grammarly, ProWritingAid, Hemingway, Ginger and others — now judged mainly on the quality of their AI passes. A practical read on where automated editing genuinely replaces a human line edit and where it still doesn't.

The Nerdy Novelist argues that authors who understand what AI is actually good at aren't the ones losing work, and walks through the parts of the fiction pipeline where AI genuinely helps versus where it reliably fails.

A short debunk of a widely-shared worry in the AI-author community, from a channel that teaches using AI to produce 12+ books a year — a window into how high-volume indie authors are actually calibrating risk right now.

Stacey Anderson explains why Codex-style agents aren't smarter models — they just have access to your files — and shows a low-stress way for authors to give an AI direct access to a manuscript project folder instead of pasting chapters into a chat box.

Viwoods' AiPaper and AiPaper Mini e-paper tablets gain a native cloud sync ecosystem with 10GB free storage, closing the loop between on-device AI note-taking and reading and a synced writing library across devices.
